content: Postgraduate education, often referred to as graduate education in North America, involves advanced study beyond a first or Bachelor’s degree. It is typically considered part of tertiary or higher education. In North America, this level of education is commonly associated with graduate schools. The structure and organization of postgraduate education vary significantly across countries and even among institutions within the same country. In some traditional German systems, there is no legal distinction between undergraduate and postgraduate education. In these systems, all education is directed toward achieving a Master’s degree, whether at the introductory (Bachelor’s level) or advanced (Master’s level) stages. The Bologna Process aims to eliminate this system to standardize higher education across Europe. Types of Postgraduate Qualifications There are four primary types of qualifications at the postgraduate level: academic degrees, vocational degrees, academic certificates and diplomas, and vocational certificates and diplomas. Degrees The term degree originates from the Latin deand gradus, meaning a step or stage, and first appeared in the 13th century. History While systems of higher education date back to Ancient Greece, China, India, and Africa, the concept of postgraduate education is rooted in the medieval European university system, which awarded degrees at different levels of study. University studies during this period required six years for a Bachelor’s degree and up to twelve additional years for a Master’s degree or doctorate. The initial six years focused on the faculty of arts, which included the seven liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music theory, grammar, logic, and rhetoric, with a primary emphasis on logic. After obtaining a Bachelor of Arts degree, students could specialize in one of three faculties—law, medicine, or theology—to pursue a Master’s or Doctor’s degree. Theology was considered the most prestigious and challenging field of study. The degrees of Master (magister) and Doctor were initially equivalent, with the former being more common in Paris and its derivative universities, and the latter in Bologna and its associated institutions. At Oxford and Cambridge, a distinction emerged between the faculties of law, medicine, and theology (which conferred the title of Doctor) and the faculty of arts (which conferred the title of Master). Theology, being regarded as the highest subject, led to the doctorate being considered superior to the Master’s degree. The primary significance of higher, postgraduate degrees was that they licensed the holder to teach. The term doctor derives from the Latin docere, meaning to teach, while magister is Latin for master and is also the root of the word magistrate. Modern Situation In most English-speaking countries, the hierarchy of degrees is as follows: Associate’s Degree: Predominantly in the United States, this degree typically requires two years of study (20 courses or 60 semester credit hours). In the UK, the equivalent is the Foundation Degree, which is worth 240 CATS credits (120 ECTS European credits). Bachelor’s Degree: Usually requiring three or four years of study (40 courses or 120 semester credit hours in the US). In some cases, a degree called bachelor may actually be a postgraduate degree, such as the Bachelor of Civil Law or Bachelor of Philosophy. In South Africa and other countries, an Honours Bachelor’s degree is awarded after a four-year program, distinguishing it from a three-year Bachelor’s degree. In France, the Licence degree is equivalent to a Bachelor’s degree, while in the Netherlands, the HBO (Hoger Beroeps Onderwijs) is equivalent to a four-year Bachelor’s education. In the UK, Honours Bachelor’s degrees are worth 360 CATS credits (180 ECTS), while ordinary Bachelor’s degrees are worth 300 CATS (150 ECTS). First Professional Degree: These degrees are required for professional licensure or entry into specific careers. They may require a Bachelor’s degree for admission, followed by three to four years of specialized study. Such programs are common in North America, while in other regions, professional education for fields like law and medicine is often undertaken through specialized undergraduate degrees or post-university vocational courses that do not confer academic degrees. In some cases, graduates are referred to as doctor, and the degree may include the word doctor in its title. In fields like engineering, the undergraduate degree (e.g., BS or BEng) is often the first professional degree. Master’s Degrees: These postgraduate degrees are sometimes organized hierarchically, starting with degrees like the Master of Arts (MA) and Master of Science (MSc), followed by the Master of Philosophy (MPhil) and Master of Letters (MLitt). In France, the DEA (Diplôme d'Études Approfondies) is a similar qualification. In fields like clinical social work or library science in North America, a Master’s degree is often the terminal degree. In the UK, Master’s degrees may be taught (e.g., MSc, MA) or research-based (e.g., MRes, MPhil). Taught Master’s degrees typically last one year and are worth 180 CATS credits (90 ECTS), while research-based Master’s degrees involve more extensive research and may last one to two years. Doctorates: These are often divided into academic and professional doctorates. Academic doctorates include the PhD (Philosophiæ Doctor) and DSc (Scientiæ Doctor). In some parts of Europe, doctorates are further divided into junior doctorates (e.g., PhD) and higher doctorates (e.g., DSc), which are typically awarded to highly distinguished professors. A doctorate is the terminal degree in most fields. In the United States, there is little distinction between a PhD and a DSc. In the UK, PhD degrees are often equivalent to 540 CATS credits (270 ECTS), though the credit structure for doctoral degrees is not officially defined. Historically, the Master’s degree was the only postgraduate degree commonly awarded, while in most European countries (except the UK), the Master’s degree nearly disappeared. However, as universities in the United States began awarding doctorates, this practice spread to the UK. Conversely, most European universities now offer Master’s degrees to align with the American model and enhance their students’ competitiveness in the international market. Honorary Degrees Many universities award honorary degrees, usually at the postgraduate level, in recognition of individuals’ achievements in their respective fields. Recipients of honorary degrees typically do not use the associated titles or letters, such as Dr. Non-Degree Qualifications Postgraduate education can also involve studying for qualifications like postgraduate certificates and diplomas, which are generally considered lower than degrees. These qualifications may serve as steps toward a degree, as part of training for a specific career, or as recognition of expertise in a narrow area of study that does not warrant a full degree program.
